factors.name: Net size
factors.summary: Size (0.99), Number of duplicate tasks (0.99) and Token split (0.96) load almost perfectly. All three grow with the number of nodes and transitions, so the factor reflects the size of the net. Density (-0.53), Coefficient of network connectivity (-0.48) and Average connector degree (-0.46) load moderately negatively, consistent with larger nets being sparser, but they are assigned to Factor 2.

factors.name: Connectivity and connector density
factors.summary: Average connector degree (0.89), Density (0.81), Coefficient of network connectivity (0.80) and Maximum connector degree (0.62) load positively, so the factor captures how densely nodes and connectors are linked by arcs. Connector Heterogeneity loads negatively (-0.72): more connected nets here tend to mix connector types less. Separability also loads positively (0.58), meaning fewer articulation points. These two loadings make the factor less clear-cut than a pure density factor.

interpretation.overall: Bartlett's test is significant and the overall KMO is 0.75, above the 0.6 threshold, so the data are suitable for a factor analysis. Two varimax-rotated factors explain 72.7% of the variance, split between net size (38.9%) and connectivity/density (33.9%). The eigenvalues (5.46, 2.20, then 0.91) support two factors, although the third eigenvalue is close to 1. Connector Mismatch stays unassigned, with a highest loading of 0.31 and a communality of 0.12. No cross-loadings exceed the gap rule. However, the three density-type measures have moderate negative secondary loadings on the size factor (-0.46 to -0.53).
caveats: Communalities of Average connector degree and Number of duplicate tasks are at the bound of the fit (possible Heywood case), so their loadings may be overestimated.
Sequentiality and Control flow complexity were removed by the MSA filter, and Number of empty sequence flows was constant, so these aspects are not represented in the factors.
Connector Mismatch is essentially unexplained by the two-factor solution.
The third eigenvalue (0.91) is near 1, so a different factor count could split Factor 2 differently.
The structure reflects shared variance in these 288 discovered nets and may depend on the discovery algorithms used, for example the very close link between duplicate tasks and size.
